resolvedQuestions.text: How do OpenBot and the other reference repos give a team conversations with a bot and an activity feed, and can a terminal or TUI match the OpenBot desktop app for that, or is a desktop shell such as Tauri worth adding?

How do the reference repos connect a bot to apps and secrets and give it a computer, compared with Skilled's MCP and Code Mode and the bots worktree isolation?

How do approvals work in OpenBot and the other repos, and what is the smallest small-team model of who can talk to, approve for and change a bot, compared with skilled bots' needs-you items and run records?

Which OpenBot parts does a small team not need (enterprise, multi-tenant, Kubernetes, managed upgrades, mobile), which code in the eight repos can be reused directly under its license, and what ranked build order should a first build packet follow?
How does an OpenBot memory reviewState (unreviewed, confirmed, edited) map onto a skilled-bots needs-you item?
How does OpenBot's vault actually store and inject a secret: what is encrypted, what a bot can see, and when a person must approve a use?
How does a terminal or TUI present a conversation with a bot together with its approvals, activity and routine list, and which repo's terminal frontend is worth copying?
How does OpenBot's app/connection registry authorize an app (OAuth client, account mode, refresh, scopes) and what would Skilled need to match it?
How should a routine's until outcome be evaluated after each run from an existing BOT.md precheck or stop expression, without adding a scheduler?
What is the smallest on-disk memory store for a few people on one machine: one JSONL per person plus a per-bot overlay?
How are conversations persisted and fanned out so several bots can share one thread, and what is the smallest activity record that can be shown after the fact?
How does an OpenBot memory source sync clock (nextSyncAt, syncStatus) map onto our cron and queue triggers?
How is OpenBot's computer provisioned and bounded (supervisor, container image, sandbox provider, per-tenant token) and what is the smallest equivalent for a small team?
What is the smallest deterministic sentence-to-trigger planner that maps routine text onto cron, queue and git-hook kinds?
How should missed routine windows and a 15-minute floor map onto launchd calendar entries and the queue drain's retry bound?
What do turnstone-main, OpenMausBot-main and rakazo-main do for apps, secrets and a bot's computer, and which of the three is simplest to copy?
What does the hermes-muse skills/companion format look like, and is it liftable as a skill store?
How does an OpenBot LearningProposal review (pending_review, approved, rejected with evidence) map onto a Skilled skill proposal?
Which OpenBot routine guardrails, the 20-enabled cap and failure-streak auto-off, belong in run records and the status index for a small team?
What is the smallest sign-in and role model for a few people sharing one machine or host, and which parts of OpenBot's owner/admin/member split and turnstone's RBAC can be dropped?
How should shared versus per-person memory be scoped when a few people use the same bots, and what does OpenBot's memory model do that skilled bots' per-bot files do not?
What is the smallest secret store skilled bots can add that keeps a value write-only, injects it without the bot reading it, and records each use in the run record?

keyFindings.text: OpenBot frames a bot as eight primitives in four pairs, and Conversations and Activity are the two ends of the work loop: Conversations is "How do I give it work?", Activity is "What did it do?". The order is fixed: Conversations, Routines, Memory, Skills, Apps, Computer, Approvals, Activity. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:6-18] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:168]

OpenBot's **app** is a connected account, not a plugin: the API describes connections as "a person's connections to apps: the accounts they signed in with so their Bots can act there for them, and an app's one shared account when an administrator connects it for everybody". [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi.yaml:63]

OpenBot's memory is a per-person fact store scoped to an organization, not a per-bot store: the collection path is `/api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/people/{personId}/memories`, so every fact belongs to a person inside one organization. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:17]

OpenBot treats a routine as one standing instruction read as a sentence in four parts: what it is, what starts it, whether it acts or only tells, and until what happens. Routines, goals and check-ins are drawn as one list although they remain three server stores. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:3-22]

Skilled bots has no memory primitive today. The `BOT.md` template's field set is `id`, `trigger`, `runtime`, `budget`, `enabled`, `delivery`, `isolation`, `sandbox`, `secrets`, `precheck`, `spec_folder`, `version` plus a body — no memory field, no store path, no recall hook. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/assets/bot-template.txt:1]

Skilled's app surface is **MCP through Code Mode**: external tools are reached by executing TypeScript against MCP servers with progressive tool loading, which gives tool access but no per-person connection record, no OAuth flow and no per-use approval. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/mcp-code-mode/SKILL.md:1]

The smallest gap-closing change is a routine layer that compiles to the existing four triggers rather than a new scheduler: an optional `routine` block in BOT.md (what, starts[], does, until), a deterministic sentence-to-block planner for the common schedule and event phrasings, `does: tell` mapped to local-only delivery plus a needs-you note, and `until` evaluated after each run from a precheck or stop expression; fatigue counting and missed-slot skipping attach to the existing run record and queue slot accounting. [INFERENCE: based on findings 4-9; OpenBot's scheduler, stores and UI are not needed, because the queue, git-hook and launchd paths already fire and claim work]

The only occurrence of "memory" in the bots-author skill is the phrase "Start from the shipped template, never from memory", which is about the author's own recall, not a bot memory feature. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/bots-author/SKILL.md:59]

OpenBot's "starts" admits a schedule, an event subscription, or a single now-run; "does" is act-within-approvals or tell-only; "until" is "you stop it" or a stated outcome that completes a goal. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:39-44] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:36-49]

OpenBot supports several bots in one conversation. The group chat is a server-owned shared transcript: the person posts once, `@Name` addresses one bot, otherwise every addressed bot runs through the ordinary headless AG-UI path one after another, and each bot answers in a thread of its own that the UI draws attributed. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/channels/group-chat.tsx:42-48]

Shared versus per-bot memory is one store with two discriminators, not two stores. `formedBy` is `person | import | bot | intelligence`, and `formedByBotId` names the bot that formed the fact; the schema says of that bot "Only that Bot recalls it." A person-formed fact has no `formedByBotId`, so every bot recalls it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:563] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:570]

The **vault** is deliberately *not* one of the eight primitives. It "sits beside the eight, in your settings", holds saved logins and keys, and "a Bot never sees what is in it"; apps and the computer "both draw on the vault, and neither keeps secrets of its own". [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:105]

A single New-routine screen writes three stores through one planner: act-on-schedule with no outcome is a routine, act-on-schedule with an outcome is a goal plus a routine, act-on-event is a goal with a subscription, now-once is a goal run at once, and tell-only is a check-in. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts:73-151]

OpenBot's activity pane is a lifecycle view, not a raw log: entries are typed as `routine`, `responsibility`, `handoff` and related kinds, each with its own icon and label, and the pane links back to the routine, task or conversation that produced the entry. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/bot-profile/activity.tsx:67-79] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:141-154]

The docs state the same split in one sentence: "Facts you add are shared with all your Bots. Facts a Bot picks up while working stay with that Bot." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:61]

The vault page is **two stores behind one page**: logins are the private sign-in form's in both editions, keys are the personal edition's own, and the team edition keeps an admin's keys under Admin while a member stores none. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/vault/vault-page.tsx:10]

A memory carries a review state of `unreviewed | confirmed | edited`, and an unreviewed memory is never recalled: "a Bot formed it or a source read it in, and no Bot recalls it until the person accepts it." Bot-formed memory therefore arrives inert and needs a human accept before it can influence a run. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:557]

OpenBot Desktop is a Tauri 2 shell whose responsibilities are the machine around the bot, not the chat itself: the manifest depends on `tauri` with `tray-icon` and `image-png`, and the entry point's module list covers install, engine, stack, update, host folder access, telemetry, recorder and uninstall. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml:28] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs:13-31]

OpenBot fires routines inside the server process: one server holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock and looks every 30 seconds, every server claims five turns at a time, and each firing is claimed from the shared work queue under a key naming its due minute so two servers cannot double-fire it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:147-161]

OpenBot's **computer** is a per-identity container with a browser, a command line and files that persist between tasks, and it is keyed by `person:<id>` or `bot:<id>`; each computer gets its own `HMAC-SHA256(COMPUTER_TOKEN, label)` so a bot that reads its own computer's token can open that computer and no other. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/shared/computer-token.ts:6]

A terminal precedent already exists in the reference set. openhuman ships `openhuman-tui`, a conversation-first terminal frontend built with ratatui and crossterm that embeds the core in-process with no HTTP server or sidecar; it covers login, saved conversations, model and agent selection, approvals, tools, child-run inspection and diagnostics. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:3-9]

OpenBot surrounds the scheduler with product guardrails: a 15-minute floor per routine, a 20-enabled-routine cap per person, one failure message per failure streak and auto-off after ten consecutive failures, and missed windows skipped rather than replayed. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:107-145]

Pausing is a boolean, not a delete: `enabled: false` means "the person has paused it. A paused memory is never recalled." Forgetting is the separate destructive operation. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:554]

The computer has a **human handoff** built in: a durable, request-scoped browser handoff with `waiting | taken | completed | cancelled | expired | interrupted`, and a secret request where a person types a value into the page and the bot never reads it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/shared/computer-control.ts:1]

Hermes Muse implements standing work as owned cron jobs with fixed cron keys and default expressions, driven by a script entry that builds a packet and lets the host run the model; a drain job batches work and re-wakes itself, and each watch job embeds its check and stop condition in the prompt. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/install.py:40-55] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/install.py:135-137] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/hooks.py:163]

Memory sources are per-bot app actions with their own sync clock. `MemorySource` requires `botId`, `toolRef` (`appId/toolName`), `args`, `enabled`, `syncStatus` (`idle | running | succeeded | error`), `syncError`, `lastSyncAt` and `nextSyncAt`; `botId` is documented as "The Bot that reads it, and the only one that recalls what it read in." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:640] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:659]

Skilled bots **declares** a posture but has no store behind it: `BOT.md` frontmatter accepts `isolation`, `sandbox` and `secrets` as three declared strings on a `Posture` block. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:52]

That TUI is a real host, not a wrapper: its event loop folds the same `web_chat` broadcast stream the desktop app consumes into `TranscriptState`, alongside a crossterm keyboard reader and a spinner ticker. The README documents `/sessions`, `/resume`, `/permissions`, `/skills`, `/mcp` and `/artifacts` as first-class commands, plus a persistent attention control for pending approvals and plan review. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/src/app.rs:8-10] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-tui/README.md:94-107]

Buzz implements event-start automation as a YAML-as-code workflow engine with four trigger types (message posted, reaction added, schedule, webhook), seven actions including request-approval and delay, and a cron loop that ticks every 60 seconds with window-based matching. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/ARCHITECTURE.md:625-670]

Memory is organization-partitioned and cannot leak across organizations: "What their Bots remember in one organization is never listed or recalled in another they belong to, and a memory named from another organization is answered as not found." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:14]

Of those three, only two are acted on. `posture.ts` resolves `sandbox` against the executor matrix and refuses a kind that cannot honor it; `secrets` is carried through the definition and never resolved to any store. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/posture.ts:99]

The other reference repos split between desktop shells and web apps: OpenMausBot is an Electron app described as "a local-first chat app for running a team of AI agents"; OpenGhost is Electron with its own hand-written UI; buzz ships a Tauri desktop plus web and admin-web; hermes-muse ships a dashboard plugin rather than an app; rakazo carries desktop, mobile, web, www, api and worker apps in one workspace. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/package.json:5] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/package.json:169] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/package.json:6] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/desktop/package.json:19-25] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/desktop/package.json:53-55] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/desktop/plugin.js:1]

A single-person OpenBot keeps no memory at all: "A single-person OpenBot keeps no memory: every operation here answers not found there." Memory is a team-edition primitive, and the docs confirm "The personal edition does not yet" list Memory. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:10] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:150]

Skilled bots' BOT.md admits exactly four trigger kinds — cron, queue, git-hook and manual — with no sentence form, no act-versus-tell field, no "until" outcome and no event subscription beyond the repository post-commit hook; cron is translated only into launchd calendar dictionaries or refused with a named invariant id. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:25-32] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:5-10] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:267-303]

Skilled bots today has no conversation surface at all. The `bots` CLI is a one-verb front door over the runtime: `run`, `disable`, `enable`, `pause`, `resume`, `inbox`, `enqueue`, `drain`, `schedule`, `answer`, `status`. The nearest thing to a conversation is `answer <item-id> <text>`, which answers a needs-you item and queues the run that continues it; the nearest thing to an activity feed is `status`, which shows each installed bot's last run, delivery and open needs-you items from the status index. [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:19-50]

Skilled's only secret machinery is a **leak guard, not a vault**: `collectKnownSecrets` harvests env vars and `.env*` values that look like secrets, and `findSecretLiteral` refuses text that contains one before it reaches a prompt, a question/answer or a delivery message. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/dispatch.ts:249]

Skilled bots already has the execution substrate a routine needs: a named file queue with rename-based single-claim and a three-attempt retry bound, a git-hook trigger that enqueues one request per matching bot on post-commit, and manual `bots run`/`bots enqueue`/`bots drain` verbs. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:1-20] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:43] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:189-201] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:23-41]

Skilled's "computer" is a **git worktree, not a machine**: a bot that declares `isolation: worktree` edits in a tree of its own, placed outside the checkout, with the launcher's shared paths linked in; there is no browser, no persistent home and no command line beyond the executor's. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/isolation.ts:5]

Verdict on terminal versus desktop for this pair: a TUI can carry all four surfaces the question names — conversations, an approvals inbox, an activity feed and a routine list — because each is text-first and event-driven, and openhuman proves the shape. What a Tauri shell adds is the machine around the terminal: a native window and tray, self-update, OS folder pickers that can grant scoped file authority, microphone capture, and supervision of a local engine or container stack. A small team that already runs the bots CLI on one machine or a shared host does not need those on day one. [INFERENCE: based on findings 2-8]

Where CopilotKit Intelligence is present, OpenBot is not the recall engine: Intelligence "holds a copy of each memory the person accepted and does the recall", and OpenBot's own record is the whole store only without it. The smallest-team reading is that OpenBot's memory is a thin record plus a delegated recall service. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:7]

`LearningProposal` requires `id`, `runId`, `operation`, `status`, `title`, `description`, `reason`, `createdAt`, `reviewedAt` and `publishedSkillId`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2124]

OpenBot connects an app once on the Connections page; the Bot never sees the sign-in, and a service that takes a key gets it from the vault. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:72-76]

OpenBot's audit trail is written before the action: every tool call returns through a gateway that resolves the target, decides it against the configured policy, writes an audit row, and only then acts — or refuses and names the rule. An action held for a person's approval writes its row when the person answers, and a forwarded action that fails writes a second row. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:7] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:41-52]

The `bots` CLI **already has thirteen verbs covering the four app surfaces**: `run` (a conversation), `inbox` and `answer` (the approvals inbox), `status` (the activity feed), and `schedule install` plus `status` (the routine list). [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:18]

Both review calls take an `IdempotencyKey` and answer 409 `LearningProposalReviewed` for a proposal already reviewed. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:1141] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:1163]

The smallest computer change is to expose the existing worktree path and branch in run records and `bots status`; the isolation and cleanup rules already exist, so no new computer implementation is needed for parity of the information a person needs. Size S, risk low. [INFERENCE: based on finding 6]

**Verdict: a CLI matches the OpenBot app experience for this slice.** The four surfaces are already four verbs, the exit codes already name the states, and the TUI is optional polish rather than a missing capability. [INFERENCE: from findings 1, 2, 3 and 8]

Verdict: skilled bots' record is already audit-grade for a single machine. Its two real gaps in this pair are the actor on a decision and a view over the record; neither needs a database, a server, or a new store. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-9]
Skilled has no proposal mechanism at all: no `proposals/` folder exists under `.skilled/skills/`, and no SKILL.md mentions one. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/ (find for proposal directories, 0 hits)]

The one existing gate a proposal would pass through is the skill-advisor's trust gate: `skill_graph_propagate_enhances` is trusted only for a real apply write (`mode=apply` with `dryRun` not `true`), and report, propose and dry-run calls stay read-safe. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skill-advisor/SKILL.md:85]
A refused trusted mutation exits 64. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skill-advisor/SKILL.md:94]

Four fields map directly: `runId` is the run record's id, `operation` is add, update or remove on a skill folder, `files` is the proposal folder's contents, and `publishedSkillId` is the skill folder name after apply. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1 through 6 and 12]

`status` should be derived, not stored, exactly as a needs-you item derives its state: `pending_review` is a proposal with no answer, `approved` is one with an answer and an applied skill, and `rejected` is one with an answer and no applied skill. [INFERENCE: based on findings 4 and 9, and the derived-state rule recorded in iteration 6]

The smallest proposal store is `{stateRoot}/{identityKey}/proposals/{proposalId}/` holding the files verbatim plus one `proposal.json`, with a needs-you item per proposal so `bots inbox` and `bots answer` stay the only review surface. [INFERENCE: based on findings 6, 11 and 15]

Approve must be idempotent and reject must be refused after approve, which the derived state gives for free: a second answer finds the item already answered and returns the same review. [INFERENCE: based on findings 8, 9 and 15]

The one thing Skilled cannot copy is the administrator check: `bots answer` has no role check today, so on a shared host anyone who can run the CLI can approve. That is acceptable for a few people on one machine and is the first thing to change on a shared host. [INFERENCE: based on findings 8 and 11]

Every audit row records on whose authority an action was taken, and a routine or a goal asserts that authority. That is the field a small-team model needs and skilled bots does not yet write. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:105]

OpenBot's computer is a browser, a command line and files that persist between tasks; it signs in with a vault login that fills the page without the Bot reading it, a page that needs the person is handed over, and folders on the person's machine can be part of the computer. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:78-84]
`runId` is "The run that proposed it." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2142]

The CLI has a **documented exit vocabulary that maps to the app's states**: 0 completed, 1 run failure, 2 usage, 3 recursion guard, 4 refused before dispatch, 5 awaiting decision. [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:54]

OpenBot distinguishes activity from the record: activity is read from the conversation's own tool results, keeps no copy of its own, and is a window; the audit trail is server-side, survives restarts, and is what an investigation reads. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/architecture.md:172]

OpenBot's vault holds saved logins and keys, a Bot never sees what is in it, apps and the computer both draw on it, and the secret stays out of the conversation and out of memory. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:105-112]
`operation` is `add | update | remove` — "Whether it adds a skill, changes one, or removes one." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2146]
`status --json` is the **machine-readable form**, so a TUI would be a renderer over an existing command rather than a new API. [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:18]

OpenBot's Activity surface covers everything allowed, refused and failed, appears in Settings for one person and Admin for a team, and a single bot's activity opens from its page beside what it is working on. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:139-154]

OpenBot's app is **forty-plus component folders** — `admin`, `approvals`, `audit`, `bots`, `browser`, `channels`, `computer`, `connections`, `decisions`, `delivery`, `desktop`, `gallery`, `learning`, `manage`, `memory`, `moves`, `needs-you`, `notifications`, `onboarding`, `passwords`, `plan`, `plugins`, `recorder`, `responsibilities`, `routines`, `settings`, `skills`, `tasks`, `team-grants`, `teams`, `vault`, `what-if`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/]

OpenBot's connectors are per-person and brokered: Composio holds the accounts, an administrator enables an app and grants actions to a Bot, each person connects their own account, and a Bot reaches the app as the person asking. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/plugins/composio.md:1-20]
`status` is `pending_review | approved | rejected`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2150]

OpenBot's needs-you surface is a board of rows plus a separate list of stalled hand-offs, which is a view over the same approval inbox rather than a second store. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/components/needs-you/board.tsx:1-40]
`publishedSkillId` is "The skill an approval published. Null until approved." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2167]

ruledOutDirections.text: Copying Buzz's YAML workflow engine wholesale: it needs a relay, Postgres and a workflow crate, which is far beyond the small-team, terminal-first scope.
Reading only `routines.md` would have missed the act/tell and until semantics that `how-openbot-works.md` states as the canonical four-part table.

Treating Hermes Muse's fixed six-job table as the target: its fixed cron keys are install-time plumbing, not a user-authored routine surface, and its event intake is limited to cron plus host session hooks.

Searching for a `vault/` or `secret/` directory at the repo root of `OpenBot-main` returns nothing; the vault lives in `app/src/components/vault/` and `app/src/components/manage/`, and the server side is behind the API rather than a named module.

Reading the generated TypeScript client under `app/src/lib/api/generated/memory/` as the model source. It is generated from `api/openapi/memory.yaml`, so the spec is the authority and the client adds no semantics.
Treating `posture.secrets` as an existing feature: grepping the runtime for `secrets` returns only the definition field and the leak guard, so there is nothing to compare against yet.

Counting "which repo has a desktop app" as evidence of a better conversation surface. Electron and Tauri shells in this set mostly wrap the same web UI; the differentiator is the host contract (streaming events, approvals, sessions), not the window toolkit.

Searching for a memory implementation directory under `api/` returned only `api/openapi/memory.yaml`. OpenBot's memory server code is not in this reference checkout, so the model must be read from the spec and docs. This bounds how far "how it is built" can be answered for memory: the contract is available, the implementation is not.

Searching OpenBot's `api/` tree for routine implementation files found only OpenAPI descriptions; the executable routine logic lives in the app and shared packages, so a server-code-only reading would have missed the planner and firing model.

Reading `OpenBot-main/docs/configuration.md` for the vault: the file is 130 KB of deployment configuration and contains no vault section, so the vault's shape had to come from the app components and the API instead.

Copying OpenBot's server-side sweep and advisory-lock scheduler: skilled bots has no server process and does not need one; launchd, the queue drain and the git hook already provide the firing and single-claim semantics for a small team.

Treating the OpenBot desktop app as the parity target for conversations: its chat UI is the same web app served to the browser, and the Tauri layer's distinctive work is engine/stack management, not chat.
Using OpenBot's mobile app as a comparison point. It is explicitly on the topic's skip list.

Looking for a ratatui, bubbletea, textual or ink TUI in every reference repo: only openhuman ships a real terminal frontend (`crates/openhuman-tui`). OpenGhost and OpenMausBot are Electron; buzz and OpenBot are Tauri; hermes-muse is a Hermes dashboard plugin; turnstone and rakazo are web/api workspaces. Repeating this survey per repo would add no new signal.

Treating `formedBy: intelligence` as a fourth memory scope. It is a provenance value for a fact the backend holds that OpenBot formed no record of, and the schema says such a fact "can be edited or forgotten but not paused" — a storage-origin distinction, not a scope.

Adding an OpenBot-style action policy engine. A bot's actions happen inside an executor whose sandbox and posture are already enforced; a second policy layer would duplicate the executor's own permission model.
A browser inside the product: the operator's own browser already has the logins, which is what OpenBot's profiles volume exists to preserve.
Applying a proposal without the skill-advisor's trusted mutation path. That path is the only write the advisor trusts, and a second write path would bypass its gate.
A Tauri shell: it wraps a web app that does not exist, and its value is packaging rather than capability.
Building a TUI now: the four surfaces are four verbs, and a TUI over `status --json` is a rendering exercise that can follow the stores rather than precede them.
Looking for an existing proposal or draft mechanism in `.skilled/skills/`. There is none: skills are authored directly, and the only staged-write pattern in the tree is the needs-you item.
A new review command beside `bots answer`. The needs-you item already carries a question, options, an answer and evidence, which is the whole proposal review.
Putting secrets in BOT.md or the prompt: the existing secret-literal check exists precisely to keep them out.
Copying Composio's broker: it is a hosted account broker with hundreds of apps, far beyond a small team's connector needs; MCP servers cover the same ground with less machinery.

Storing `status` as a field on the proposal. Every value is readable from the answer and the applied skill, so a stored copy could disagree with them, which is the same failure the needs-you item avoids.
Adding a separate audit database. The run record, delivery entry and result event already form the trail; a second store would be the first place to drift.
Embedding evidence in the proposal. OpenBot serves evidence from its own endpoint so a reviewer reads it on demand; embedding it would make every proposal carry its whole transcript.
Looking for activity in the status index beyond rows and flags: the index is a summary, not an event log.
Copying the approvals board as a TUI screen. The board is a filtered list over the inbox; `bots inbox` already lists the same items.
Looking for an audit row in skilled bots' run record: the run record has the outcome and evidence, but not a per-decision row.
Treating the worktree as a full computer would overstate parity: it has files and commands, not a browser or a vault-filled login.
Searching BOT.md for an apps or vault key found none; the definition has posture fields but no connector surface.
Building a browser-driving computer from scratch: OpenBot's browser and handover are a large surface, and the worktree already gives a Bot a real command line and files.
Looking for a terminal UI in the other seven repos: none ships one. OpenMausBot is Electron, OpenBot is Tauri plus a web app, and the rest are servers or CLIs without a TUI.
A sign-in system: it would be a second identity beside the one every path already uses, and the first thing it would have to do is agree with `identityKey`.
Searching the other seven repos for a terminal UI. Only openhuman ships one; OpenBot, buzz and openhuman's own app are Tauri, and OpenGhost and hermes-muse are desktop shells.
Sharing one memory file for everything: OpenBot's split between person-added and bot-learned facts is the useful boundary, and collapsing it would leak one bot's working notes to the others.
Building a Tauri shell first. OpenBot's native side exists to install and supervise Compose, and a runtime that boots in-process has nothing to install or supervise.
Shipping a mobile client before a terminal client exists. The terminal is the stated preference and the smaller build.
Looking for a single-user mode in the Kubernetes chart: the personal edition is the single-user mode, and it is explicitly not the chart.
Per-person secret stores: they would break the shared-account case, which is the common case for a small team and is OpenBot's own `shared` account mode.
Looking for a mobile web build in the phone app: it is a native React Native project, not a responsive web page.
Searching skilled bots for a user or role model found only repository identity and the per-user state root; there is no user account to extend.
Copying openhuman's four tabs as-is. Logs, Chat, Config and Settings are its own split; the OpenBot surfaces are conversations, approvals, activity and routines.
Treating the team edition as a small-team feature would overstate its fit: its admin scope is a many-person policy layer, not a few-person permission model.
Building a password store or SSO for a few people: OS users and file permissions already separate state, and a sign-in adds a credential surface with no matching threat.
A "lite" multi-tenant mode. Tenancy is in the URL space and the database schema; a lite version would be a second product.
A web UI served from the CLI. The TUI needs no HTTP server or sidecar, and a served UI would add a port, a session and a browser to a tool that already runs in the terminal.
Looking for a per-person key in the state root: there is none. `identityStatePaths` keys by identity only, and `retired` records identities rather than people.
Adopting the Helm chart as the small-team install path. It installs a cluster workload with a management agent and a licence requirement.
Copying OpenBot's "Everyone" admin scope: it administers many people's access to eight primitives, which is more than a small team needs.
Three roles: OpenBot's own `owner` is not assignable, so a small team's two roles are the same shape with the deployment owner implicit.
Treating the terminal as a reduced client. openhuman's TUI drives the same `web_chat` surface as its desktop app, so the surface is shared rather than reimplemented.
Copying OpenBot's React approval cards. The logic is in `shared/`, the cards are presentation tied to the web app.
Lifting anything from openhuman: GPL-3.0 is copyleft, and a permissive product cannot absorb it.
Treating OS notifications as desktop-only would overstate the gap: a terminal can emit them, but it cannot show a tray or an embedded browser.
Per-bot memory ownership. OpenBot scopes memory to the person and the organization, and a per-bot store would make a person's facts disappear when the bot is renamed.
Looking for a NOTICE file in OpenBot: there is none, so MIT attribution is the only obligation.
A session token or cookie. The state root's owner and mode already decide who can read and write, and a token would be a second authority that can disagree with the filesystem.
Copying OpenBot's Tauri app: it is a full installer/updater/engine manager, far larger than a small team's terminal-first scope.
Looking for a role or permission check anywhere in the runtime. There is none: `bots answer` writes the answer after a secret check and nothing else.
Copying openhuman-tui code. GPL-3.0-only would force the combined work under GPL.
Lifting turnstone's OAuth runtime: it is Python, and the per-user path is dark by default, so the rule is worth more than the code.

Looking for a TypeScript secret store in OpenBot: there is none. OpenBot's vault is server-side and its client only renders forms, so the only liftable TypeScript store in the eight repos is rakazo's.
Looking for a permissive memory implementation in openhuman: GPL-3.0 rules it out for direct reuse.
Three roles. `admin` governs people, sign-in and policy; with no sign-in there is nothing for it to govern, so it collapses into `owner`.
Lifting openhuman-tui code: GPL-3.0 makes it a design reference only.
Copying hermes-muse's kernel state machine. It is MIT but Python and coupled to a host plugin API; the state vocabulary is the reusable part, not the code.
Building a desktop shell first: the four app surfaces are data views a TUI can render, and the desktop's extra value is delivery and browser embedding rather than missing primitives.
Looking for a terminal UI in OpenBot found none; its app is web and its desktop shell is Tauri, so the terminal reference has to come from another repo.
Copying OpenBot's connection registry: it is an OpenAPI description of a server this product does not have, so the shape transfers and the code does not.
Building sign-in. OpenBot's own single-person install has none, and a few people on one machine already have an OS identity that a session would only duplicate.
Building the terminal client first. It would draw four empty surfaces until the memory, review, proposal and routine items exist.
Starting with the secret store: it is the largest slice and the only one that can leak, so starting there puts the risk first and the proof last.
Keeping the multi-tenant memory scope. A small team is one organization, so the second scope would be a branch nothing takes.
Building memory in this packet: it is another pair's share and it couples to nothing here.
Lifting OpenBot's desktop shell. Its native side installs and supervises Compose, which this runtime does not have.
Building the desktop shell first: the terminal can render every app surface, and the desktop's extra value is delivery and browser embedding.
Treating the eight parts as independent. Conversations, activity and approvals share the run record and the actor field; building them in the ranked order avoids writing that record three times.
Building all four slices as one packet: the first two prove the design, and the last two depend on what the first two learn about the run record.
Lifting openhuman's TUI code. GPL-3.0 cannot be relicensed into this tree, so only the shape transfers.
Starting with apps and the vault: connectors widen a Bot's reach, so they should come after approvals and activity give a person a way to see and stop what a Bot did.
Looking for one OpenBot component that could be lifted wholesale. The value is distributed across small pure modules and policy documents; the UI is not portable.
Looking for a dependency that forces the secret store before the connector registry: there is none. The two share only the `grants` field, which is slice 4 and can land after both.
Any enterprise, multi-tenant, Kubernetes, managed-upgrade or mobile work (iteration 11).
A single "big bang" parity packet: the eight parts touch different subsystems, and one packet would be too large to verify.
Looking for a permissively licensed terminal client to lift. The only one in the set is openhuman's, and it is GPL-3.0.
Starting with the conversation surface: it is the largest new surface and depends on a memory and role story that the routine packet does not.
A desktop-first build. Iteration 1 found that OpenBot's chat surface is the web app and its Tauri layer is engine and update management.
A server or database for conversations, memory, skills or activity. Each maps to files the runtime already writes, and the queue already provides atomic claims.
Treating the reuse list as a dependency list: most candidates are design references or small functions, not packages to install.
Using OpenBot's admin "Members do it themselves" setting as a template for a role system. It is a per-action-kind switch, not a role.
Modelling the three origins as three storage locations. All three produce the same `Skill` record; only the proposal path adds a staging row, so the origin is provenance rather than a separate store.

Treating "saved login" and "credential" as one store: they have different owners, different permissions and different use paths, so a parity build needs both or an explicit decision to ship one.
Copying OpenBot's owner/admin/member roles into skilled bots. With no sign-in and no tenant, the roles have nothing to distinguish; the same protection comes from recording who approved what.
Copying turnstone's full RBAC and permission-string model. It exists to let an administrator delegate across many users and endpoints, a problem a small team does not have.

Lifting openhuman code directly: its GPL-3.0 license would impose copyleft on the combined work, so it is a design reference only.
Looking for a client-side decryption path: every read endpoint returns metadata only, so there is nothing to decrypt in the app. The secret never leaves the server except into a page field.
Reading OpenBot's deployment doc alone would have suggested Kubernetes is the normal path; the minimum-size and single-container sections show the one-host path is fully supported.
Treating `bots answer` as an approval system. It continues a parked run; it does not gate an action before it happens.

Adopting OpenBot's Kubernetes charts or managed-upgrade agent for a small team: both solve fleet problems (per-person computers, many installs) that a single host does not have.

Treating `tools` on a skill as a capability grant. The schema says naming an action gives no bot access to it, so a skill cannot be used to escalate a bot's reach and does not need a grant check at approval time.

Adding a goal store to evaluate outcomes: a single `until` command per routine is enough for a small team, and OpenBot's goal graph is only needed for multi-routine goals.
Treating the run record's `exit.reason` as an outcome signal would conflate "the run completed" with "the routine's goal is met"; those are different facts and need different fields.
Building a second memory store beside the host's. hermes-muse explicitly declines to, and the reason is structural: two stores drift and the model cannot tell which is authoritative.
`app/src/components/connections` is a UI surface over the same endpoints; it added no new contract facts beyond the three connect outcomes already in the API description.
Building a web UI first. Every surface the question names is a list or a transcript, and the runtime already stores both; a browser adds a server and a session layer without adding information.
Looking for an existing post-run hook in the runner found only delivery and worktree cleanup; the terminal path has no outcome-evaluation stage today.
Evaluating `until` on failed runs: a failed run has no outcome to judge, and treating its failure as "not met" would hide the failure behind a routine continuation.
Copying OpenGhost's hand-written drawing engine or OpenMausBot's Electron shell. Both are large UI codebases tied to a desktop runtime.
Reusing `precheck` as the until field: it runs before dispatch and its silent marker skips a run, which is the opposite of completing a routine.
Treating the OAuth client as the normal path: it is the exception for vendors that refuse dynamic registration, so a parity build should not start there.

Copying hermes-muse's `SKILL.md` frontmatter as a skill record. It carries three fields and no scoping, so it cannot express who may use a skill or which bot offers it; the OpenBot `Skill` record is the better shape and the Skilled `SKILL.md` frontmatter is already richer.
Searching openhuman-tui for a separate approvals screen: approvals are overlays and a status control, not a page. The overlay is the model to copy.

Copying turnstone-console. It solves multi-node cluster visibility, a problem this team does not have.

Looking for a refresh-token endpoint: there is none. Refresh is implicit in the connection record plus `confirmConnection` and `recheck`, which re-ask the app rather than rotating a token the client holds.
Looking for a routine list in openhuman-tui: it has `/sessions` and `/skills` but no routine concept; OpenBot's four-part row is the better source.
Treating every event phrase as a git-hook: only repository events map to the existing hook; mail and other external events need a queue producer, and claiming otherwise would overstate parity.
Treating the computer as a sandbox mode: it is a separate service with its own image, entrypoint, volumes and token. A sandbox flag on an executor cannot stand in for it.
Reusing OpenBot's planner directly: `planRoutine` maps form answers to OpenBot's routine/goal/check-in stores, not to skilled bots' trigger union, so only its four-part shape transfers.
Looking for an activity view in the status index: it stores rows and flags, not a lifecycle grouping.
Using a model to parse routine sentences at run time: it adds nondeterminism and a model call to an authoring step that a closed phrase table can cover.

Looking for a skill-proposal path in OpenGhost. Its skills are discovered from folders and installed from a link; there is no proposal queue. The "proposed from use" origin remains an OpenBot-only pattern in this repo set.

Treating OpenGhost's `by` field as a review gate. An agent-written record is live at once; the user's control is edit and remove, not approve. That is a different trust posture from OpenBot's `reviewState` and the difference matters for the recommendation.
Searching for a natural-language parser in skilled bots found only the cron reader; there is no text-to-schedule layer to extend.
Assuming gVisor is the boundary: it is opt-in, and the documented default is an ordinary container sharing the host kernel. The real boundary is the container plus the per-computer token.
Copying openhuman's memory subsystem. It is a vendored engine with a job queue, a document brain and a source registry, and it is GPL-3.0. For a small team it is the wrong size and the wrong licence.
Treating the run record as an activity log. It is one record per run; a conversation needs several messages per run.
Reading OpenMausBot's `routine-cron-text.ts` as a parser would be wrong: it renders cron to a sentence, and the reverse direction lives in Rakazo's `cronFromPreset`.

Searching for a `supervisor/` or `agent-computer/` directory in this checkout: both are published images referenced by name, so their source is not here. The compose file's comments are the contract, and they are unusually explicit about why each setting exists.

Building a server-side group transcript with per-bot threads, as OpenBot does. Skilled bots runs one bot per dispatch in a worktree; the file-chain model already preserves attribution without a message server.
Looking for a message table in skilled bots' runtime: there is none. Delivery entries record where a result went, not what was said.
Reusing OpenBot's channel/member tables directly. They assume a multi-tenant organization and a database, neither of which this team needs.

Looking for a shared "vault" module across the three: each solves it differently (Postgres table, Fernet store, external password manager), so there is no single thing to lift. The reusable part is the *shape*, not the code.
Copying turnstone's OAuth stack wholesale: it is a Python service with a Fernet keyring and a per-server admin form, sized for a multi-node deployment rather than a few people on one host.
Treating the drain's retry bound as a missed-window policy would conflate "this attempt failed" with "this occurrence is too old to run"; the two are different facts.
Copying the owner/admin/member split. Owner and admin are the same authority in OpenBot's own helper, so the three names collapse to two behaviours, and a few people do not need a delegation tree.
Building the "recorded from a demonstration" origin. It needs a recorder, a container per person and an external analysis service, which is the enterprise shape D3 puts on the skip list.
Treating any of the three as a connector catalogue: none ships a catalogue of apps; rakazo and turnstone both assume you bring the service, and OpenMausBot assumes you bring the password manager.
Applying the launchd slot policy to queue requests unchanged: a queue request has no schedule slot, so it needs its own staleness bound rather than the launchd grace window.
Replaying every missed occurrence: both OpenBot and the existing slot accounting explicitly reject a backfill burst.
Adding a new missed-window mechanism for cron: slot accounting already implements skip-not-replay with lateness classes and skipped-slot evidence.
Adding Better Auth or any identity provider. OpenBot needs it because it serves many organizations over the network; a small team on one host already has an identity in the OS or SSH layer.
Copying OpenMausBot's computer: it is an Electron desktop shell driving a native CUA driver, which is the desktop path D4 deprioritises and the largest possible lift.
Searching for a floor in the installer or definition schema found none; the only schedule guard is the translator's exact-translation rule, which accepts every-minute expressions.
A separate shared-memory store and per-bot memory store. No reference repo does it, and it doubles the write path for no gain.

Searching Skilled for an existing memory store to extend. There is none: the only continuity surface is the spec-kit's per-packet `handover.md` and `_memory.continuity`, which is per-packet, not per-person or per-bot. The gap is real and cannot be closed by configuration.
Copying OpenBot's `reviewState` as a three-value enum with an `edited` state. Two values (`unreviewed`, `confirmed`) carry the gate; `edited` is a UI affordance, not a recall rule.
Copying turnstone's permission strings. They exist to let an administrator compose custom roles across endpoints; a small team needs one gate, not a policy language.
Treating the status index as an identity source: it is keyed by repository identity, not by person.
Looking for a user table in skilled bots' state root: there is none, only per-identity repository state.
Looking for an existing encryption helper in the runtime: there is none, so the key handling has to be specified rather than reused. Turnstone's config-only rule is the cheapest correct answer.
Searching skilled bots' runtime for memory code: there is none, and the library README's module table confirms the absence rather than a gap in the search.
Reusing `NeedsYouItem` verbatim for memory review. Its `id` is the run id and its open state holds the bot, so a single unreviewed fact would stop every later run of that bot.

Looking for a non-holding item class in `needs-you.ts`. There is none: `holdForBot` returns a hold for any open item of the bot, so a non-holding review item is a new shape rather than a configuration of the existing one.
Reusing the drain backoff as the fatigue rule: the drain backoff protects the drain job from a broken setup, not a bot from a repeating failure.
Reading OpenBot's memory components (`memories.tsx`, `sources.tsx`) for a data model: they are screens over the API, not the model.
Adding a third `edited` review state. The answer text already carries the rewrite, so a third state would need its own transition rules for no recall benefit.
Searching for existing streak or cap code found only slot-summary and cron-dictionary caps, which bound evidence size rather than bot behavior.

Building a memory service or embedding store. The reference set's service-shaped memories (OpenBot Intelligence, openhuman CortexDB) exist to serve many users and machines; a few people on one host do not need recall ranking.
Copying OpenBot's per-person Learning containers. They depend on a hosted backend and a skills marketplace; the same value comes from a proposed SKILL.md reviewed in a packet.
Giving each bot its own memory schema. The BOT.md contract is already a stable, small frontmatter; memory belongs beside the bot, not inside its definition.
An external password manager like OpenMausBot's Bitwarden: it adds a service, a CLI dependency and a sync loop for a team of a few people.

A separate review UI. `bots inbox` already lists open items and `bots answer` already resolves them; a second surface would be the "two pages answering the same question" that OpenBot's own rules forbid.
A proxy-injection like rakazo's `secret_request`: it needs a server that makes the outbound call, which skilled bots does not have and a small team does not need.
Adding a fatigue counter to each BOT.md definition: the definition is authored state, and the count is runtime history that belongs with run records.
A page-field injection like OpenBot's masked box: skilled bots has no browser, so there is no field to fill. The command variable is the equivalent primitive.
Making the fatigue stop a silent disable: OpenBot posts a final message, and a silent stop would leave a person wondering why the routine stopped.
Treating `exitReason` alone as a streak signal would miss refusals that are not failures; the check must count only terminal failed runs.

A second SQLite database for memory. The index is SQLite because it answers cross-identity queries; memory is read whole by one bot at a time, so a database would add a schema and a migration for no query benefit.
One JSONL per person. The runtime's atomic write helper is whole-file, so JSONL buys nothing and costs a new append path plus a line-level parser.
Keying memory by repository identity only. That is what the runtime does today, and it makes a person's facts vanish when they move to another checkout.
Looking for an existing per-bot MCP filter: there is none. The launcher is a pass-through, so the filter has to be added at the config-file level rather than inside the launcher.
Copying OpenBot's action-recognition table wholesale: it is tuned to browser and app tool names, and skilled bots' executor exposes a different tool surface.
A connector catalogue: none of the eight repos ships one that a small team would use, and the UTCP config already names the servers this team actually has.
Copying OpenBot's goal store and subscription tables. The same behaviour comes from a BOT.md field plus the existing queue, without a database.
Looking for an existing per-person key to hang memory on. There is none: `identityKey` is derived from `owner/name`, and no other identity dimension exists in the runtime.
Reusing the definition-approval hash as an action-approval policy: it proves which bytes may run, not which actions a run may take.
Replaying missed windows. OpenBot's stamp model is better than a backlog, and skilled bots' slot accounting already summarizes missed slots instead of running them.
Copying the 15-minute floor and 20-enabled cap as server rules. They are product guardrails for a chat-driven authoring surface; a small team authors bots in files and can see the whole list.
Treating the queue as a general event bus. It carries run requests with an idempotency key, not arbitrary events.
Treating `bots status` as an activity feed would lose chronology; it is a snapshot of last run and delivery, not a list of events.
Searching skilled bots for a per-action approval policy found only the definition-approval module and the executor sandbox, which operate at different layers.
Building an OAuth server: it is the largest single piece of OpenBot's app layer and the one a small team can skip, because a shared account or a key covers the common case.
Per-person connections: they need a sign-in surface and a session store. A small team on one host can share one account per app, which is OpenBot's own `shared` account mode.
One JSON file per fact, matching `records/` and `needs-you/`. A memory of a few hundred facts would become a few hundred files, and recall would read the whole folder on every run.
Adding a new approvals database: needs-you items already model the parked-run question and answer, and the status index already indexes them.
Looking for a routine scheduler in skilled bots beyond launchd: cron translation and launchd installation are the whole scheduling layer.
Copying OpenBot's browser computer (live screen, take-the-wheel, recorder). It is the largest surface in OpenBot and the least needed by a team whose bots work in repositories.
Storing `syncStatus` as a field. Every one of its four values is already readable from the queue and the last run record, so a stored copy could disagree with them.
Treating the needs-you resume path as a chat loop would lose the conversation transcript, because a needs-you item holds one question and one answer, not a history.
Building a desktop shell first: the terminal can show conversations, approvals, activity and routines from existing stores, and a desktop shell adds delivery mechanics rather than missing primitives.
Storing `nextSyncAt` as a computed timestamp. The runtime deliberately reports `UNKNOWN` for a next fire because no launchd surface reports one, so a stored value would be a guess that goes stale.
A separate sync scheduler beside the drain job. The drain job already runs on a throttle with backoff and already claims requests from the inbox.
Replacing the worktree with a container per bot. The worktree is cheaper, already audited, and the posture matrix already refuses unsafe combinations.
Reusing the existing headless run path unchanged for chat: its prompt explicitly says nobody is at a prompt, so a chat surface needs a different prompt contract and a conversation store.
Building an administrator grant table for apps. With one operator group and a file-defined bot, the bot's own secret allowlist is the grant.
Lifting openhuman-tui code: GPL-3.0 would impose copyleft, so it is a design reference only.
Looking for an app catalogue in skilled bots: MCP servers are configured outside the bot runtime, in Code Mode's own configuration.
gVisor: OpenBot itself leaves it unset by default, and the executor kinds that matter already give an OS boundary.
Looking for a next-fire calculator in the runtime. There is none by design: `NEXT_FIRE_UNKNOWN` is the only value the installer ever reports for `nextFire`.
A profiles volume: the operator's own browser profile is the profiles volume, and it is already logged in.
Looking for a vault in skilled bots' runtime: secrets come from the process environment and dotenv files, with literal scanning, not from a store.
A fifth trigger kind for memory sync. The four kinds already cover a timed read-in, and a new kind would need its own validation, install path and drift rule.

Looking for a browser capability in the executor matrix: there is none. `EXECUTOR_WEB_SEARCH_CAPABILITY_MATRIX` covers web *search*, not a browser, so a headed browser is not something any executor kind can be asked for.
Searching the bots CLI for a conversation verb found none; the CLI is a run-control surface, not a chat surface.
A per-bot container: it is the largest piece of OpenBot's computer and it exists to serve a browser farm. A small team runs one bot at a time on one machine.
Looking for a skill registry in the bots runtime: there is none; skills live in the Skilled tree, and the bot runtime does not read them.
Loading every skill into every prompt: skill bodies are long, so BOT.md must name the few it needs.
A new delivery channel for approvals: `desktop` is the only channel and it does not acknowledge, so the honest move is to fix the acknowledgement rather than add a channel.
Building memory now: it couples to nothing, so it can be added at any time and should be added last.
Copying OpenBot's automatic-learning pipeline: Intelligence containers, per-person spaces and sharing review are enterprise-scale machinery, not a small-team need.

Looking for a memory module under a different name (`context`, `notes`, `knowledge`): the runtime has none. The nearest thing is the spec-kit's own packet documents, which are per-spec rather than per-bot.
Searching hermes-muse for a skill-proposal or skill-creation mechanism. There is none: the companion skill is authored, never generated, and the only staged-write path is for memory.
Treating the spec-kit's continuity writer as per-bot memory would conflate project continuity with a Bot's own knowledge.
A separate proposal UI. hermes-muse reviews a staged write with a slash command and an id, which is the same shape as `bots inbox` plus `bots answer`.
Searching BOT.md for a memory or skill key found none; the definition has no such surface today.

Lifting the companion folder as a template. Its 21 references are all Muse domain pages (goals, dispatch, proactivity, sources, calendar, weather, feed, briefings), so copying the folder would import a domain, not a format.
Looking for a per-person skill scope in the spec-kit: the packet is the scope, not the person.
Making memory a model-written free-for-all: the smallest store is a person-authored shared file plus a per-bot file, with a needs-you item when a Bot wants to add a fact.
Building a skill marketplace or a Learning container. Both exist in OpenBot to distribute skills across many people; a small team installs skills by moving a folder.

A database-backed skill store. hermes-muse keeps skills as markdown and state in SQLite, and the skill is explicitly forbidden to hand-edit that database; a skill store in a database would invert that split.
Adding a `grants` table to the status index: the index is a projection of files, and a grant is already in the run record, so a table would be a second source of truth for the same fact.
Storing learned skills in the BOT.md body. The body is the standing instruction; a skill is a separate, reviewable, reusable unit.
A new frontmatter schema. Skilled's five keys already cover what the companion's three do, and adding a key would need a discovery-rule change for no gain.
Giving skills their own storage format. `SKILL.md` with frontmatter already holds everything a proposed skill needs.
